source: Sellier, Scopelliti, Morewedge (2019) Debiasing training improves decision making in the field (published abstract) + Corrigendum 2020
finding: The published abstract says trained students were 19% less likely to pick the confirming option. PubMed lists a Corrigendum (Psychol Sci 2020 Jun;31(6):762) as erratum for this paper.
numbers: N=290; 19% fewer inferior confirming choices. PubMed records the corrigendum (PMID 32423341, doi 10.1177/0956797620930211, one page).
quote: Trained participants were 19% less likely to choose the inferior hypothesis-confirming solution than untrained participants.
limits: The corrigendum text itself could not be opened (publisher blocks fetch). That the 29% to 19% change came from the corrigendum is an inference from d02 plus d01, not read.
agent_relevance: Use 19%, not 29%, as the field-transfer effect size for the human anchor.

source: Sellier, Scopelliti, Morewedge (2019) accepted manuscript, City Research Online
finding: The accepted manuscript still said 29%. The design was not randomised: training date varied with the class schedule. Effect did not decay between short and long lag. Effect ran through fewer confirming arguments.
numbers: Trained n=182, untrained n=108. Short lag 11 days (n=125) vs long lag 43-52 days (n=57): 56.8% vs 63.2%, chi2(1)=.65, p=.419. 22 untrained (20.4%) never played the game. With confirming and disconfirming arguments in the model, the intervention term fell to p=.509.
quote: Trained students were 29% less likely to choose an inferior hypothesis-confirming solution
limits: Natural-experiment assignment, graduate business students, one case. Gender mix differed (73.1% vs 63.0% male, p=.071). Same authors as the original lab game.
agent_relevance: Human field evidence is one quasi-experiment; do not treat 'training transfers' as a replicated law. The mechanism (fewer confirming arguments) fits a scaffold step that makes the agent list disconfirming arguments.

source: Sellier, Scopelliti, Morewedge (2019) The Conversation summary
finding: The authors' own summary says 'a single field experiment', no replication outside it, and that they do not know why this game transferred better than other training (engagement, practice with feedback, or how biases were explained).
numbers: 29% (pre-correction figure); 62% trained before the case; mean gap 18 days; game window 20 days.
limits: Press piece by the authors, not independent. Shows the 29% figure circulated before the correction.
agent_relevance: Confirms gap 3 and 8 are open in the authors' own view: component and independent replication are unknown.

source: Heerma van Voss, Yoon, Scopelliti, Zweet, Helsloot, Morewedge (2025) Debiasing training reduces confirmation bias in national risk analysts, Sci Rep
finding: Analysts and students were tested before and after one training session. Both improved. The design has no untrained control group, and two authors (Scopelliti, Morewedge) are the original game team.
numbers: Pre-post effect general domain F(1,168)=104.6, partial eta2=.384; risk domain F(1,168)=46.0, partial eta2=.215. Complete observations: analysts 56 (78.9%), students 116 (98.3%). Analysts showed less confirmation bias than students at pretest.
limits: Pre-post only, same session, so practice or test-retest effects are not separated. Not an independent replication. Claim K06 overstated it as a replication.
agent_relevance: Treat as supporting but weak evidence for expert transfer; no long-term retention here.

source: Morewedge et al. (2015) Debiasing Decisions, accepted manuscript (re-read for component structure)
finding: Game and video differ in several ways at once: games had all four Fischhoff procedures (teach bias, teach direction, feedback, extended feedback with coaching) and practice; videos had only the first two plus strategies, passive. So the game-over-video gain cannot be assigned to feedback alone. Game variants (score, narrative examples, hints, full vs first round only) did not differ.
numbers: Game: -46.25% and -31.94% at once, -34.76% and -23.57% at 2-3 months (Exp 1, 2). Video: -18.60% and -25.70% at once, -20.10% and -19.20% later. Variant tests: Exp 1 F<=2.29, p>=.13; Exp 2 t<=1.77, p>=.08. Half of Exp 1 game players played only the first round.
quote: more research is needed to determine precisely why it was more effective
limits: Non-significant variant tests are low-power null results, not proof of no effect. The authors say more research is needed to learn why the game worked.
agent_relevance: A single round of practice plus an after-action review seemed as good as three rounds, so a short, one-time feedback block may be enough for an agent. Which ingredient matters is unknown.

source: Lyu et al. (2025) SACD, ablation tables (gpt-3.5-turbo)
finding: Removing the bias-analysis step or the bias-determination step each raises bias a lot; removing both (= self-help rewrite) is worst. So the detect-analyse-rewrite loop beats a single rewrite in this setting.
numbers: Average bias score, SACD vs w/o determination vs w/o analysis vs w/o all: FOMC 0.1175 / 0.1890 / 0.2370 / 0.3490; PubMedQA 0.0560 / 0.3030 / 0.2660 / 0.2880; LegalBench 0.0965 / 0.2180 / 0.3020 / 0.4590. Multi-bias FOMC: 0.1220 vs 0.3520 without determination.
limits: Ablation only on gpt-3.5-turbo, 500 samples per setting. Tokens and cost were NOT equalised; SACD uses up to 3 passes, self-help one. Bias score is the authors' own metric.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 only partly closed: the loop wins, but at unmatched compute. A matched-token test (self-help sampled 3 times and majority vote) is still missing.

source: Lyu et al. (2025) SACD, error analysis and iteration curves
finding: SACD removes 'insufficient debiasing' errors but creates two new error types: judging an unbiased prompt as biased, and naming the wrong bias type. In finance, iteration 1 was worse than vanilla; gains come at iterations 2 and 3.
numbers: Errors out of 500: self-help 257 / 209 / 409 (finance / medical / legal); SACD total 61 / 111 / 79. SACD misjudgment 12 / 3 / 6; confusion 49 / 108 / 73. Finance average bias: vanilla 0.1648, self-help 0.1885, SACD iter1 0.2070, iter2 0.1460, iter3 0.1175. Max iterations set to 3.
limits: Misjudgment here is a false alarm on prompts that are unbiased in the data set; accuracy cost of the rewritten prompt was not reported. gpt-3.5-turbo, Llama-3.1 and gpt-4o only; no reasoning model tested.
agent_relevance: False alarm rate of a detect step is small (0.6-2.4%) but the wrong-type rate is large (10-22%). A scaffold detector should be checked on clean items.

source: Lyu et al. (2025) SACD, baseline comparison on gpt-4o (FOMC)
finding: On gpt-4o, few-shot debiasing made bias much worse than vanilla, while self-help and SACD were near zero and Reflexion helped moderately. Giving worked examples of debiased answers is not a safe substitute for the model checking its own prompt.
numbers: gpt-4o FOMC average bias (100 samples): vanilla 0.3650, few-shot 0.3975, CoT 0.3650, Reflexion 0.2450, debate 0.3700, zero-shot debiasing 0.2650, few-shot debiasing 0.7350, self-help 0.0625, SACD 0.0300.
limits: n=100 for gpt-4o; one task domain shown. Few-shot debiasing examples are static, not feedback on the model's own errors, so this is only adjacent to gap 1.
agent_relevance: Static examples can backfire; no LLM study here gives the model feedback on its own earlier errors. Gap 1 stays open.

source: Sovrano, Dominici, Bacchelli (2026) Mitigating prompt-induced cognitive biases in general-purpose AI for software engineering (PROBE-SWE)
finding: Generic prompts (chain of thought, self-debiasing) gave no significant per-bias reduction after correction. CoT was worse than no prompt. A method that first elicits best-practice axioms and injects them cut bias sensitivity about half; hindsight was the exception.
numbers: Median bias sensitivity: baseline 12.9%, CoT 16.1%, implication prompting 13.3%, impersonated self-debiasing 10.2%, imperative self-debiasing 10.3%, both together 8.3% (-4.6 pp; no per-bias test significant after FDR, all q>=.07). Axiom method: about -51% on average (p<.001), up to -73% for some biases. DeepSeek-R1 row: baseline 16.3%, CoT 18.5%, best about 6.6%.
limits: Software-engineering dilemmas, cost-effective models plus DeepSeek-R1; sensitivity = answer flips between biased and unbiased wording, not accuracy. Longer prompts add cost; risk of over-regularisation noted by authors.
agent_relevance: Supports adding the correct norm (what a good decision uses) rather than only warning. Reasoning model R1 was still biased, so reasoning alone does not remove prompt-induced bias.

source: Jhaveri, GX-Chen, Sucholutsky, Choi (2026) Failing to Falsify: confirmation bias in language models
finding: This is the paper behind claim K16 (identity now confirmed). Eleven LLMs show confirmation bias in a 2-4-6 rule-discovery loop. Dual-Goal and Think-in-Opposites prompts raise success on average from 42% to 56%, but gains are significant only for thinking models.
numbers: Success 6% to 78% across models (max 45 turns). Think-in-Opposites improved success in all 11 model-by-mode cases, Dual-Goal in 8 of 11. Incompatible-to-compatible test ratio rose in 18 of 22 cases. Non-thinking models: no significant change in ratio, small drop in accuracy for Dual-Goal. Distilling the behaviour almost tripled success cross-scale.
limits: Number-triple task; one alternative per turn, so it does not test how many alternatives to list (gap 6). Distillation is training, out of our scope.
agent_relevance: Consider-the-opposite works for the agent when it has long reasoning; for short-reasoning modes it can do nothing or hurt slightly.

source: Sanna, Schwarz, Stocker (2002) When debiasing backfires: accessible content and accessibility experiences in debiasing hindsight, JEP:LMC
finding: Listing 10 ways an event could have turned out otherwise made hindsight bias worse; listing 2 produced no hindsight effect. The felt difficulty of generating many alternatives was read as 'few alternatives exist'.
numbers: Two studies; participants listed 2 (easy) or 10 (hard) counterfactual thoughts. 10 thoughts consistently increased hindsight bias; 2 thoughts gave no significant hindsight effect.
quote: Listing many counterfactual thoughts was experienced as difficult and consistently increased the hindsight bias
limits: Human participants and one bias (hindsight). No LLM test of ease-of-generation was found. An LLM has no felt difficulty, so the mechanism may not transfer; output length and the quality drop of late alternatives may still matter.
agent_relevance: Ask for 2-3 strong alternatives, not 10. Test the number as a parameter in the agent.

source: Sanna and Schwarz (2003) Accessibility experiences and the hindsight bias, Memory & Cognition
finding: Replicated the backfire with a second manipulation (brow contraction, a bodily difficulty cue). Listing many thoughts about known outcomes had the opposite effect ('it could never have happened').
numbers: Exp 1: many vs two thoughts; Exp 2: brow contraction. Many alternative thoughts made the known outcome rated MORE likely.
limits: Hindsight only. Same research tradition; a task variant but not an independent lab.
agent_relevance: Direction of the thought list matters: many alternatives to the known answer can overshoot the other way. Cap list length.

source: Branchini, Burro, Bianchi (2023) Training people to think in opposites facilitates falsification in Wason's rule discovery task, J Intelligence
finding: A short 'think in opposites' training raised the share of people who found the rule and sped up discovery, mainly by getting them to test descending triples.
numbers: Training group beat control in proportion discovering the rule and in speed (abstract; exact counts not read).
limits: Abstract only. One task; content-free training, so transfer to other tasks was not shown.
agent_relevance: Human basis for the Think-in-Opposites prompt used in d10. Supports a one-alternative contrast step rather than a long list.

source: Wang et al. (2026) Making Bias Non-Predictive: Epistemic Independence Training (RL), Qwen3-4B
finding: Training on bandwagon cues only transfers to other content cues (authority, distraction) but not to structural cues (answer position). Prompt-based mitigation can wreck clean accuracy. Training on wrong-bias cases alone teaches a shortcut that hurts when the cue is right.
numbers: Distraction wrong-bias robustness 40.6% to 79.7% (+39.1); authority 68.5% to 72.9%; position-B 38.6% to 36.4%. Prompt mitigation: Qwen3-4B clean accuracy 66.2% to 40.9% (validation). SFT: Qwen3-1.7B clean accuracy 84.3% to 52.1% (test). Wrong-only: bandwagon wrong-bias 63.6% to 84.2% but correct-bias 90.4% to 71.2%. Without independence reward wrong-bias robustness 80.0% to 65.8%.
limits: Weight training with RL, small Qwen3 models, MMLU-Pro; not in-context. No in-context-practice arm, so gap 9 is only half answered.
agent_relevance: Cross-family transfer is real inside the 'content cue' family and absent for structural cues. Any cue-ignoring step must be tested on cases where the cue is correct, to avoid learning to reject all hints.

source: Huang et al. (2026) CogBias: measuring and mitigating cognitive bias in LLMs (steering and prompt debiasing)
finding: Judgment and information-order biases resist prompt debiasing and need strong steering; social and response biases respond to prompts. Steering learned on one family transfers to another about as well as within family, but random directions also lower bias, and cross-model transfer fails.
numbers: Steering gives 26-32% bias-score reduction. Prompt debiasing: judgment -4.4% (backfires), response +40.5%. Qwen capability loss -19.0 pp (judgment) and -10.8 pp (info processing); Llama under 1 pp. Same-family r=-0.14 vs cross-family r=-0.13, p=.61. Learned directions only 1.6% better than random.
limits: Open-weight Llama-3.3-70B and Qwen2.5-72B; capability check in one analysis used a coarse 10-question probe. Activation access needed, so not usable for a scaffold-only agent.
agent_relevance: Supports bias-family-specific mitigations; do not expect one generic prompt to cover judgment biases.

source: Raj et al. (2026) Debias It Yourself (DIY): five human intervention procedures taught to LLMs
finding: Training on gender examples with human-derived procedures (stereotype replacement, imaging, individuation, perspective taking, positive contact) lowered bias on held-out dimensions too, with every procedure transferring a little. Differences among the five procedures were small.
numbers: Reasoning accuracy on Balanced COPA and ARC stayed at or above base on Qwen3.5-27B. Held-out transfer positive for all five; positive contact strongest, stereotype replacement weakest. Revision at inference gave most of the reduction; training alone smaller and less consistent.
limits: Social stereotype bias, not judgment biases. LoRA training involved. Exact percentage cells sit in figures I did not read as numbers.
agent_relevance: Cross-dimension transfer holds for social stereotypes after procedural training; no test for confirmation to anchoring (gap 4 still open for judgment biases).

source: Yang et al. (2025) Rethinking prompt-based debiasing in large language models (BBQ)
finding: Debiasing prompts make models over-flag bias in clean text and hide behind 'Unknown'. Lower bias score then reflects avoidance, and accuracy falls where the context gives the answer.
numbers: Models flagged bias in disambiguated (unbiased) contexts persistently; bias score stayed under about 6% while accuracy in disambiguated contexts fell. Removing the 'Unknown' option exposed the avoidance.
limits: BBQ social-bias benchmark; exact table cells not copied here. Judgment-bias tasks may differ.
agent_relevance: Measure false alarms and accuracy on clean items with every debiasing step (gap 5): bias score alone rewards refusing to decide.

source: Cognitive Biases in Large Language Models: A Systematic Quantitative Assessment and Debiasing Analysis (Electronics 2026)
finding: Eleven biases, eight modern models, over 70,000 responses. Significant bias in 27 of 43 bias-model pairs, but only one pair survives a test that needs the effect to hold across prompt rewordings. Three prompt debiasers (zero-shot CoT, adversarial counter-prompt, role prompt) have bias-dependent effects.
numbers: 27 of 43 (62.8%) significant after multiple-comparison correction; variant-level test: 1 significant. N=100 trials per configuration. Models include GPT-4.1 Mini, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Gemini 2.5 Flash, DeepSeek V3.
limits: Only the abstract was available (publisher blocked full text); debiasing numbers not read.
agent_relevance: Much measured LLM bias depends on prompt wording; debiasing tests need several paraphrases or they overstate effects.

source: Algorithmic Anchoring: how prompt-embedded reference points bias LLM financial estimates (SSRN 2026)
finding: In 51,000 calls to three recent commercial models, labelling an anchor as 'a prior AI estimate' raised anchor sensitivity by 52%. GPT-5-mini anchored far less than Claude Haiku 4.5 and Gemini 2.5 Flash.
numbers: Slope 0.272 to 0.413 (+52%); 51,000 API calls; fictional companies.
limits: Abstract only; SSRN preprint, one author; no debiasing prompt tested.
agent_relevance: Recent models still anchor and source labels matter: an agent's own earlier output, labelled as its estimate, may anchor it (relevant to gap 7).
